name: The Age of Fires
summary: The discovery that held the world together, and the argument that came with it.
body: The discovery, when it finally came, was so plain that it embarrassed everybody who had spent centuries on the sea theory.
The things people talk about stay.

That is the whole of it. A thing remembered by one person alone holds its shape for a while and then begins to go. A thing spoken about — told, aloud, to somebody who is actually listening — holds very much longer, and a thing told often enough by enough people does not go at all. The high crossings over the gorge have stood through everything because for a great many years there was never a week when somebody was not telling somebody else about the crossings over the gorge.
What followed is remembered as the Age of Fires, and it was the best of us.

The fires were lit — real ones, because you cannot get people to sit down and listen in the dark and the cold — and there was a rota. That word does not sound like the foundation of a civilisation, but that is exactly what it was. Somebody was responsible for each fire. Somebody walked a circuit between them. When a star came down, a keeper went to it, told the new arrival what had happened to them, and asked for their name and one true thing while they could still say it, and then carried that name to the next fire and said it there.
Whole districts of Nangijala were held up, stone by stone, by people who were good at talking in the evening. Some of them are still standing.
It is worth being honest about the flaw, because everybody here has an opinion about it and a new star will be asked their view within a month.

A told story grows. It is retold slightly warmer, slightly braver, slightly better shaped, every time, by people who mean nothing but well. Keep a man alive by telling him for forty years and at the end of it you have a man — solid, present, in no danger of going anywhere — who is not quite the man who fell. The fire-keepers know this. Most of them have decided it is a price worth paying, and a few of them have decided it very defensively.

So there came a second party, who said: write it down. Set it down exactly, once, and it is safe from all of you. And they were right, and they were thorough, and they made the Chronicle, which is the book you are reading now.

And then they found the thing that nobody has yet explained. A person recorded perfectly — every detail fixed, nothing drifting, the record sitting there entire and correct — goes Quiet anyway, on the usual schedule, with their own complete and beautiful account open on the shelf beside them.
The fire-keepers say the reason is obvious and that they have been saying it the whole time. It was never the accuracy. It was the listening.

The Chroniclers, who are not fools, have never accepted this, because it is not an explanation, it is a slogan. The argument is unresolved. It is the only argument in Nangijala that everybody has taken a side in, and you will be asked.
